themes.definition: External or internal audit of AI systems, controls or submissions, and requirements that systems be auditable.
themes.what_is_set_out: Binding audit duties in this cell are narrow: notified bodies audit providers' quality management systems periodically (Annex VII), and the Omnibus gives the AI Office remote and on-site inspection powers. The European Court of Auditors commits, as external auditor, to 'actively scout EU systems that incorporate AI components', to 'examine the quality and reliability of the information systems, data and – where applicable – algorithms used by our auditees', and to keep its guidance on auditing AI in line with INTOSAI and ISACA practice. EU043 suggests that national laws on police biometric identification let the authorising authority audit submitted information, 'including the technical details and accuracy criteria', before and after use, and let supervisory authorities check the stop-and-delete afterwards. The EDPS and JRC documents say systems should be auditable (explainability is needed so that 'The AI system is auditable'; processing should be 'traceable and auditable'; generative AI 'must be transparent, explainable, consistent, auditable and accessible'; services must 'meet auditability standards'), without saying who audits or against what. ENISA recommends that national authorities require critical infrastructure operators to attest zero-trust baselines and AI incident escalation paths in annual audits, and proposes machine-processable security attestations; this is an edge case, since it concerns AI used by attackers rather than AI tools used by public bodies.
themes.holders: Notified bodies; the AI Office; the European Court of Auditors (as external auditor and in its own guidance); authorising authorities and supervisory authorities (EU043); EUIs and organisations (EDPS); public administrations (JRC, unnamed); critical infrastructure operators and national authorities (ENISA).
themes.binding: Statutory for notified-body audits and AI Office inspections; commitments and strategic goals for the ECA ('will'); suggested national-law content (EU043); non-binding 'must' and 'necessary to ensure' in EDPS guidance; 'it is crucial' (JRC); recommendations (ENISA). Consequences are not stated outside the AI Act.
themes.checks: ECA audit of auditees' algorithms: trigger: audit planning (not stated per system); compared against: 'quality and reliability' (no criteria given); metric or threshold: not stated; who: the ECA; what happens with the result: not stated. Police biometric identification audit (EU043 suggestion): trigger: any time before or after use; compared against: the submitted technical details and accuracy criteria; metric: not stated; who: the authorising authority; result: not stated. Notified-body audit: periodic, against the quality management system; result: an audit report to the provider. ENISA attestation: trigger: annual audits; compared against: zero-trust baselines; who: operators attest to national authorities [inference]; result: not stated. The EDPS names 'consistent' as a required property of generative AI systems but gives no metric or test.

quotes.location: The ECA’s strategic AI goals, para 20 (p. 8)
quotes.quote: examine the quality and reliability of the information systems, data and – where applicable – algorithms used by our auditees in the EU’s financial management and governance;

quotes.location: PDF p.9 (printed p.8), s.2 (information box on 't…
quotes.quote: generative AI systems must be transparent, explainable, consistent, auditable and accessible, as a way to ensure fair processing of personal data.

As services become more automated, it is crucial to maintain transparency, human oversight and accountability, in order to uphold public trust and meet auditability standards, in accordance with the requirements of the AI Act.
Require critical infrastructure operators to attest zero-trust baselines, resilient incident response capabilities during annual audits, and clear escalation paths for AI-accelerated incidents.

themes.theme: Accountability conditions on real-world testing and sandboxes
themes.definition: Answerability, registration, consent, reporting and liability conditions on providers testing AI in regulatory sandboxes or in real-world conditions.
themes.what_is_set_out: Testing a high-risk system in real-world conditions may go ahead only if the provider has submitted a testing plan to the market surveillance authority, registered the test (with a Union-wide identification number and the Annex IX information, or in the non-public section for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border uses), is established or represented in the Union, and has the subjects' informed consent (Art. 60(4), 61). Before consenting, subjects must be told 'the arrangements for requesting the reversal or the disregarding of the predictions, recommendations or decisions of the AI system' (Art. 61(1)(d)), and they may withdraw at any time without detriment or justification. Member States give market surveillance authorities powers to demand information and make unannounced remote or on-site inspections; serious incidents are reported under Art. 73; suspension, termination and final outcomes are notified; and providers are liable for damage caused in testing. In regulatory sandboxes, participants remain liable to third parties but face no administrative fines if they follow the plan and the authority's guidance in good faith; a short summary of each project is published on the authority's website (except sensitive law enforcement, border, immigration or asylum data), while exit reports are published only if provider and authority both agree. The Omnibus requires national frameworks for its new Art. 60a testing to 'include effective governance and accountability arrangements', without defining them, and makes the national competent authority the supervisor of that testing.
themes.holders: Providers and prospective providers (testing and in sandboxes); market surveillance authorities; national competent authorities; Member States; test subjects and their legally designated representatives.
themes.binding: Statutory conditions: testing may not proceed if they are unmet. Civil liability under Union and national law; the sandbox fine exemption is conditional on good faith; publication of exit reports is optional; recitals use 'should'.
themes.checks: Authority checks on testing (Art. 60(6), 76): trigger: during testing, including unannounced inspections; compared against: Art. 60 and the testing plan; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the market surveillance authority (the national competent authority for Art. 60a testing); what happens with the result: not stated in these passages. Subject challenge of outputs (Art. 61(1)(d)): trigger: a test subject's request; compared against: not stated; metric: not stated; who: not stated, because the arrangements are not specified; result: reversal or disregarding of the AI system's prediction, recommendation or decision.

quotes.quote: the provider or prospective provider has drawn up a real-world testing plan and submitted it to the market surveillance authority in the Member State where the testing in real world conditions is to be conducted
the arrangements for requesting the reversal or the disregarding of the predictions, recommendations or decisions of the AI system

provided that the prospective providers observe the specific plan and the terms and conditions for their participation and follow in good faith the guidance given by the national competent authority, no administrative fines shall be imposed

quotes.location: Art. 1(25), inserting AI Act Art. 60a(5)(c); p. 25
quotes.quote: (c) include effective governance and accountability arrangements;

themes.theme: Publication by regulators and advisory bodies
themes.definition: Duties on the Commission, the AI Office, national authorities, notified bodies and advisory bodies to make reports, decisions, lists and interests public.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission publishes annual reports on police real-time biometric identification based on aggregated national data and excluding sensitive operational data (Art. 5(7); EU043 notes that locations and cameras used may be withheld), will publish Member States' laws on such use, publishes and updates the list of systemic-risk general-purpose models, and makes its Art. 112 evaluation reports public. The AI Office and the Board publish their assessment of codes of practice (the Omnibus gives this to the Commission), and under the Omnibus the AI Office publishes its commitment and non-compliance decisions, naming the parties and 'including any penalties imposed'. National competent authorities publish their annual sandbox reports or abstracts online and short summaries of sandbox projects, while exit reports are published only by mutual agreement. The advisory forum publishes an annual activity report, scientific panel experts publish declarations of interests, notified bodies publish lists of subsidiaries, and sectoral good practices under the transparency code are published 'to enable monitoring'. [inference] Publication by regulators is mostly aggregated and subject to confidentiality and law enforcement carve-outs, so it reveals little about any particular public body's tool.
themes.holders: The Commission; the AI Office and the Board; national competent authorities; the advisory forum; scientific panel experts; notified bodies; code Signatories and associations setting sectoral good practices.
themes.binding: Statutory duties ('shall'); a Commission commitment ('will', EU043); optional publication by mutual agreement (sandbox exit reports); code commitment ('will', EU121). Consequences are not stated.

quotes.quote: The Commission shall publish annual reports on the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, based on aggregated data in Member States

quotes.location: Art. 1(32), inserting AI Act Art. 75d(4); p. 33
quotes.quote: The AI Office shall publish the decisions it adopts pursuant to Articles 75b and 75c. Such publication shall state the names of the parties and the main content of the decision, including any penalties imposed.

If both the provider or prospective provider and the national competent authority explicitly agree, the exit report may be made publicly available through the single information platform referred to in this Article.

The AI Act requires the Commission to publish annual reports of the uses of real-time RBI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes in the Member states and by Union institutions, agencies and bodies, based on aggregated data.

themes.theme: Publication of general-purpose model training-content summaries
themes.definition: The duty on general-purpose AI model providers to publish a summary of the content used for training on a mandatory template, and how its accuracy is checked.
themes.what_is_set_out: All general-purpose model providers, including open-source ones, must 'draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary' of training content on the AI Office's template (Art. 53(1)(d), Recital 107; EU088 para 23). The Explanatory Notice (EU090) makes the template 'a common minimal baseline': general information; the main datasets, listing large public datasets (over 3% of the public data for that modality) and private ones; a narrative of scraped data with the top 10% of domain names by content size (for SMEs the top 5% or 1,000 domains); and data-processing aspects such as measures to respect text-and-data-mining opt-outs. The summary must cover all training stages from pre-training to alignment, but not input data used during the model's operation, and must be published on the provider's website and distribution channels when the model is placed on the market. It must be updated whenever further training on new data requires it (at six-month intervals or sooner if materially significant), is limited to the modification data for downstream modifiers, and for models on the market before 2 August 2025 is due by 2 August 2027, with any gaps 'clearly disclosed and justified'. Providers should report 'in good faith and in an accurate and comprehensive manner'; the AI Office may verify whether the template was filled in correctly, without a work-by-work assessment, request corrective measures and fine up to 3% or EUR 15 000 000. EU090 also recommends voluntary answers to rightholders' requests and encourages alternative dispute resolution such as mediation.
themes.holders: Providers of general-purpose AI models (including open-source providers and SMEs); downstream entities that modify a model; the AI Office (verifies); rightholders and other parties with a legitimate interest.
themes.binding: Statutory duty with a mandatory template; EU090's explanations are non-binding interpretation ('should'); fines of up to 3% of worldwide turnover or EUR 15 000 000; voluntary disclosure to rightholders and ADR are only recommended or encouraged.
themes.checks: AI Office verification: trigger: not stated (discretionary 'may'); compared against: the template and Art. 53(1)(d); metric or threshold: not stated, and no work-by-work assessment; who: the AI Office; what happens with the result: corrective measures and fines. Update trigger: further training on additional data, at six-month intervals or sooner if materially significant; this is the only passage in the cell that ties an accountability duty to a change in the model version.

quotes.quote: draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training of the general-purpose AI model, according to a template provided by the AI Office
The AI Office may verify whether the Template has been filled in correctly in order to assess if the provider has complied with Article 53(1)(d) AI Act .

The Summary should also be updated whenever the provider further train s its own general-purpose AI model placed on the market on additional data that requires an update of the content of the Summary.
Such instances must be clearly disclosed and justified in the copyright policy and in the summary of the content used for training.

themes.theme: Transparency of public administrations' AI use to citizens (non-binding)
themes.definition: Recommendations that public administrations explain to citizens when, where and how AI is used and how it shaped decisions, and voluntary transparency measures beyond legal minimums.
themes.what_is_set_out: The JRC handbook (2022) says public administrations' use of AI should meet 'the highest possible level of transparency', that 'Citizens and businesses need to be able to understand when, where and which AI based solution is used, and to which extent AI use has influenced any decisions affecting them', and that the exercise of public powers should be 'controlled through public administrative law'; it asks how citizens can know an administration applies compliance models, and says shared success and failure cases need 'fully enforced transparency procedures'. The JRC's 2025 report says administrations 'have a duty to provide clear details about the data, processes and decision-making involved in AI solutions', suggests algorithmic registries and outreach on benefits and risks, and says transparency, human oversight and accountability must be kept as services become more automated. The ECA commits to tell its auditees about its own use of AI for data analysis 'whenever necessary', a term it does not define. The EDPB lists voluntary measures beyond GDPR information duties: public communications on collection criteria and all datasets used, transparency labels, model cards, annual transparency reports, and publishing the legitimate-interest balancing test. None of these passages names a binding duty-holder or a consequence; the 'duty' in JRC143539 is framed as part of the public-sector mandate, not as a legal obligation [inference].
themes.holders: Public administrations and the public sector (JRC); the European Court of Auditors; controllers (EDPB, optional measures).
themes.binding: Recommendations and suggestions ('need to', 'could', 'might', 'it is crucial'); an ECA commitment ('will', 'whenever necessary'); optional measures that supervisory authorities may take into account (EU074). No consequence is stated.

quotes.quote: Citizens and businesses need to be able to understand when, where and which AI based solution is used, and to which extent AI use has influenced any decisions affecting them.

Public administrations have a duty to provide clear details about the data, processes and decision-making involved in AI solutions, enabling individuals to understand and trust these solutions and how they are used by public administrations.
transparency labels and model cards the systematisation of which could structure the presentation of information on AI models, and annual transparency reports on a voluntary basis.
we will proactively communicate with our auditees about our use of AI for data analysis whenever necessary, ensuring transparency and fostering trust throughout the audit process.

themes.theme: Telling people that AI is in use or is deciding about them
themes.definition: Duties to inform individuals that they are interacting with AI, are subject to a high-risk AI system's decision, or are exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, together with data protection information duties.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers must design systems that interact with people so that people are told they are dealing with AI, unless that is obvious (Art. 50(1)); the Commission's Art. 50 guidelines say this applies to police chatbots on official websites and crime-reporting hotlines despite the law enforcement exception, and that AI agents must disclose both 'their artificial nature and the person on whose behalf they are acting'. Deployers of Annex III high-risk systems that make or assist decisions about people must tell them they are subject to the system (Art. 26(11)) and, per Recital 93, about their right to an explanation; employers, including public bodies [inference], must tell workers and their representatives before using a high-risk system at work (Art. 26(7)). Deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation must inform the people exposed, including children (Art. 50(3); EU_Art50). Under data protection law, EU institutions must give individuals all required information when generative AI processes their personal data and meet transparency duties to people whose data they scrape, chatbots may need specific notice that no human is involved, controllers owe data subjects 'meaningful information', and information on AI processing should be 'accessible, understandable and user-friendly' (EU074). Breaches of Art. 50 are fineable up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%, and up to EUR 750 000 for Union bodies.
themes.holders: Providers of AI systems that interact with people, including AI agents and public crime-reporting systems; deployers of Annex III high-risk systems that decide about people; deployers who are employers; deployers of emotion recognition and biometric categorisation systems; EUIs and other controllers.
themes.binding: Statutory duties in the AI Act (Arts 26 and 50), fineable via Art. 99(4)(e) and (g) and Art. 100 for Union bodies; recitals use 'should'; Commission guidelines are non-binding interpretation; EDPS and EDPB passages restate statutory GDPR/EUDPR duties or use 'may require'.

quotes.quote: deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III that make decisions or assist in making decisions related to natural persons shall inform the natural persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system
Such systems may be used , but they remain subject to the transparency obligation under Article 50(1) AI Act, so natural persons must be informed they are interacting with such systems.
AI agents must be designed and developed in such a way that they disclose both their artificial nature and the person on whose behalf they are acting

quotes.location: PDF p.29 (printed p.28), s.11 Informing individua…
quotes.quote: EUIs must provide to individuals all the information required in the Regulation when using generative AI systems that process personal data.

themes.theme: Explanation of AI-assisted decisions, human intervention and contest
themes.definition: Rights of affected people to an explanation of the AI system's role in a decision, to human intervention and to contest the decision, and internal commitments to explainability.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act gives a person affected by a deployer's decision based on the output of an Annex III high-risk system, where the decision has legal or similarly significant adverse effects, the right 'to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken' (Art. 86, Recital 171). Under the EUDPR, where generative AI supports automated decisions, EU institutions must guarantee at least 'the right to obtain human intervention', to express a view and 'to contest the decision', and the EDPS says the duty to give meaningful information about the logic involved 'should generally be extended' to decisions that are not fully automated but include automated preparatory acts; its CV-screening example requires information about the system's logic and envisaged consequences. The EDPB only points to Art. 22 GDPR without analysing it. The European Parliament's internal frameworks require that AI reasoning be made 'transparent and understandable so that it is then clear why a model led to a certain recommendation or suggestion' (EP2024, proposed) and call for 'a specific communication process concerning explainability' (EP2020). By contrast, the AI Act's Recital 59 names 'the difficulty in challenging their results in court' for suspects facing law enforcement AI but sets out no mechanism; and in real-world testing, subjects must be told how to request reversal or disregarding of the AI's outputs (Art. 61(1)(d)).
themes.holders: Deployers of Annex III high-risk systems (owe explanations); affected persons (right-holders); EUIs as controllers; the European Parliament administration (internal frameworks); providers in real-world testing.
themes.binding: Art. 86 is a statutory right, with the consequence of breach not stated in the Article ([inference] a complaint to the market surveillance authority); the EUDPR safeguards are statutory duties restated by the EDPS, while the extension to preparatory acts is a non-binding interpretation; EP2024 uses 'shall' in a proposed internal framework; EP2020 is an internal guideline; Recital 59 is non-binding and gives no holder or mechanism.
themes.checks: Human intervention (EUDPR): trigger: a decision based solely on automated processing, extended by the EDPS to automated preparatory acts; compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the controller; what happens with the result: the decision can be contested and reviewed by a human. Explanation (Art. 86): trigger: the affected person's request; who: the deployer; result: an explanation of the AI system's role and the main elements of the decision. Neither route says which cases must reach a human before a decision is taken.

quotes.quote: shall have the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

quotes.location: PDF p.30 (printed p.29), s.12 Automated decisions
quotes.quote: they need to ensure that individual safeguards are guaranteed, including at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to contest the decision.
This obligation should generally be extended to cases where, although the decision procedure is not entirely automated, it includes preparatory acts based on automated processing.

quotes.location: page 3, II. Compliance and control, para 14
quotes.quote: The reasoning behind AI algorithms and decision-making processes shall thus be made transparent and understandable so that it is then clear why a model led to a certain recommendation or suggestion.
